stem:
A 77-year-old woman attends her GP for a blood pressure check. She has capacity. When asked how things are at home, she becomes upset and says that her grandson, who moved in last year, has been taking money from her pension and she is scared to challenge him because he loses his temper.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Tell her that family money matters are outside the GP's professional role
options.B: Assess her safety and follow adult safeguarding procedures, involving her
options.C: Advise her to change her bank PIN and take no further safeguarding action
options.D: Arrange a joint appointment to discuss the concern with her grandson present
options.E: Record the conversation in her notes but take no further action at this stage

correct_answer: B. Assess her safety and follow adult safeguarding procedures, involving her
why_correct: Financial abuse is a recognised form of abuse under the Care Act 2014, and her fear of her grandson's temper raises concern about her wider safety. The GP should listen, check whether she is in immediate danger, explore her wishes and follow local adult safeguarding procedures. Because she has capacity, she should be involved in decisions, although information can still be shared without consent if there is a serious risk to her or others. Source: Care and support statutory guidance (chapter 14, safeguarding), Department of Health and Social Care, Care Act 2014.
why_wrong: A. Financial abuse is a safeguarding issue and clinicians have a duty to respond. C. Practical advice alone leaves an adult at risk without support or protection. D. Discussing the allegation with the alleged abuser present could put her at greater risk. E. Documentation without action does nothing to protect her.
pearl: Financial or material abuse is one of the categories of abuse listed in the Care Act 2014 statutory guidance, alongside physical, sexual, psychological, neglect, discriminatory, organisational, domestic and modern slavery.
thinking: Older adult discloses money being taken ↓ Fear of the person responsible ↓ Financial abuse is a safeguarding category ↓ Assess immediate safety and her wishes ↓ Follow adult safeguarding procedures
exam_trap: E, Documenting and taking no action — recording the disclosure feels responsible, but on its own it leaves her exposed to ongoing abuse.
takeaway: A disclosure of financial abuse by an older adult needs a safeguarding response, not just advice or a note.

stem:
On a busy medical take, a registrar asks a first-year foundation doctor to carry out a diagnostic lumbar puncture alone while the registrar sees other patients. The foundation doctor has watched the procedure once but has never performed it or been trained in it.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Go ahead carefully and document clearly in the notes that it is a first attempt
options.B: Do it as asked, because the registrar who delegated it holds the responsibility
options.C: Read the trust's procedure guide on the ward first, then perform it unsupervised
options.D: Explain they are untrained and ask for supervision or a competent colleague
options.E: Watch an online video of the technique on the ward computer before starting alone

correct_answer: D. Explain they are untrained and ask for supervision or a competent colleague
why_correct: Doctors must work within the limits of their competence. Being asked by a senior does not transfer that responsibility, so the foundation doctor should explain honestly that they are not trained and ask either to be supervised or for someone competent to do it, which also serves as a training opportunity. Source: Good medical practice (domain 1, knowledge, skills and development), General Medical Council, 2024.
why_wrong: A. Documenting a first attempt does not make an unsupervised, untrained procedure safe. B. A senior's request does not override the duty to work within competence. C. Reading a guide is not training and does not confer competence. E. A video cannot replace supervised practice.
pearl: GMC Good medical practice states that doctors must recognise and work within the limits of their competence, even when a more senior colleague asks them to act.
thinking: Asked to do an untrained procedure ↓ Senior request does not transfer responsibility ↓ Patient safety comes first ↓ Explain limitation honestly ↓ Request supervision or a competent operator
exam_trap: B, Doing it because the registrar asked — hierarchy makes it feel expected, but each doctor remains responsible for working within their own competence.
takeaway: Never perform an untrained procedure alone; say so and get supervision or a competent colleague.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman with ileal Crohn's disease diagnosed ten years ago attends the emergency department with her fourth episode in a few months of colicky central abdominal pain after meals, followed by vomiting and bloating that settles after a day or two. She has no fever and her inflammatory markers are only mildly raised.

Which complication best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Long-standing transmural inflammation in Crohn's disease heals with fibrosis, narrowing the bowel lumen, most often in the terminal ileum. This produces recurrent post-prandial colicky pain, vomiting and distension from partial obstruction. Only mildly raised markers suggest a predominantly fibrotic rather than active inflammatory narrowing, which may need endoscopic dilatation or surgery. Source: Crohn's disease: management (NG129), NICE, 2019.
why_wrong: B. A perianal abscess causes local pain, swelling and fever rather than obstructive symptoms. C. Toxic megacolon is an acute colonic emergency with systemic toxicity, not recurrent self-settling episodes. D. Gallstone ileus is a rare cause of obstruction in older women and would not recur in this pattern. E. An enterovesical fistula between bowel and bladder causes pneumaturia, faecaluria and recurrent urinary infections.
pearl: MR enterography is the usual imaging for assessing small bowel Crohn's strictures because it avoids radiation in young patients who may need repeated scans.
thinking: Long-standing ileal Crohn's disease ↓ Recurrent colicky pain after meals ↓ Vomiting and bloating that settle ↓ Low inflammatory activity ↓ Fibrotic stricture with partial obstruction
exam_trap: C, Toxic megacolon — it is a well-known IBD complication, but it is a colonic emergency with systemic toxicity rather than recurring episodes of post-prandial obstruction.
takeaway: Recurrent obstructive symptoms in long-standing Crohn's disease suggest a stricture.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with alcohol-related liver cirrhosis and known ascites is seen in the medical admissions unit. Over two days she has developed a low-grade temperature, diffuse abdominal tenderness and mild new confusion, and her ascites has increased.

Which investigation is the most important to perform without delay?

options.B: CT of the abdomen with contrast
options.E: Abdominal ultrasound to measure liver size

why_correct: Fever, abdominal tenderness and worsening encephalopathy in a patient with cirrhotic ascites should be treated as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis until proved otherwise. A diagnostic tap for neutrophil count, culture and other analysis is the key test, and British Society of Gastroenterology guidance advises a diagnostic tap in everyone with cirrhosis and ascites who is admitted, so that antibiotics can be started promptly if confirmed. Source: Guidelines on the management of ascites in cirrhosis, British Society of Gastroenterology and British Association for the Study of the Liver, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Endoscopy looks for varices but does not investigate infected ascites. B. CT may help if secondary peritonitis is suspected but does not diagnose spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. D. Ammonia levels add little to the clinical assessment of encephalopathy and do not identify its cause. E. Measuring liver size does not answer whether the ascites is infected.
pearl: An ascitic neutrophil count above 250 cells per cubic millimetre is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
thinking: Cirrhosis with ascites ↓ Fever, abdominal tenderness, new confusion ↓ Suspect spontaneous bacterial peritonitis ↓ Diagnostic tap for neutrophil count and culture ↓ Start antibiotics promptly
exam_trap: D, Serum ammonia — the confusion tempts a focus on hepatic encephalopathy, but the encephalopathy here is likely being triggered by infection that needs diagnosing.
takeaway: Any deterioration in a patient with cirrhotic ascites warrants a diagnostic ascitic tap to look for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
notes: Reviewer fix: Diagnostic tap on admission attributed to NICE NG50; corrected attribution to BSG ascites guidance.

stem:
A 55-year-old woman attends the emergency department after a night of repeated vomiting. Her serum lipase is several times the upper limit of normal. Before labelling this as acute pancreatitis, the registrar wants a clinical feature that fits the diagnosis.

Which finding in her history would best support it?

options.A: Intermittent colicky right loin pain that spreads down into the groin
options.B: Painless yellowing of the skin with a palpable gallbladder
options.C: Fresh red blood mixed in with her stools
options.D: Constant severe upper abdominal pain radiating through to the back
options.E: Sharp central chest pain eased by sitting forward

correct_answer: D. Constant severe upper abdominal pain radiating through to the back
why_correct: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when two of three criteria are met: characteristic abdominal pain, amylase or lipase at least three times the upper limit of normal, and typical imaging findings. She already has the biochemical criterion, so constant severe epigastric pain radiating to the back would complete the clinical picture and make imaging unnecessary for diagnosis. Source: Pancreatitis (NG104), NICE, 2018, with the revised Atlanta classification of acute pancreatitis, 2012.
why_wrong: A. Colicky loin-to-groin pain suggests renal colic. B. Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder suggests malignant distal bile duct obstruction such as pancreatic head cancer. C. Fresh blood in the stools points to a lower gastrointestinal source. E. Pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward suggests pericarditis.
pearl: The height of amylase or lipase does not correlate with severity; severity is judged by organ failure and scoring systems such as the Glasgow-Imrie criteria.
thinking: Lipase raised more than three-fold ↓ Diagnosis needs two of three criteria ↓ Need typical pain or imaging ↓ Constant epigastric pain to the back is the typical pain ↓ Supports acute pancreatitis
exam_trap: B, Painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder — it is a pancreatic-sounding finding, but it suggests pancreatic head malignancy rather than acute pancreatitis.
takeaway: Acute pancreatitis is confirmed by typical epigastric pain plus enzymes at least three times normal, or imaging if either is missing.

stem:
A 38-year-old man tells the practice nurse that on some days he gets bloating, cramps and loose stools after meals, and he wonders whether he is intolerant of something in his diet. Between episodes he feels well, and he has no weight loss or bleeding.

Which part of the history will be most helpful in assessing a possible food intolerance?

options.A: The result of a commercial IgG food-antibody test he bought online
options.B: The result of a hair analysis test from a high-street health shop
options.C: The timing of symptoms in relation to particular foods eaten
options.D: His ABO blood group, to match him to a 'blood-type' diet
options.E: His childhood vaccination record and any reactions to vaccines

correct_answer: C. The timing of symptoms in relation to particular foods eaten
why_correct: Assessing food intolerance relies on identifying which foods precede symptoms, how soon after eating they start, and whether they are reproducible. A food and symptom diary is a practical way to capture this. This history guides any trial of exclusion and helps separate intolerance from allergy or other gut disease. Source: Food intolerance, NHS website (nhs.uk), accessed October 2026.
why_wrong: A. Commercial IgG food-antibody tests reflect normal exposure to foods, not intolerance, and are not recommended. B. Hair analysis has no evidence base for diagnosing food intolerance. D. Blood group has no role in diagnosing food intolerance, and blood-type diets are not evidence based. E. Vaccination history does not help identify a dietary trigger.
pearl: Unlike IgE-mediated allergy, food intolerance is usually dose-related and delayed, and there is no reliable blood test for it.
thinking: Episodic gut symptoms after meals ↓ Well between episodes, no alarm features ↓ Possible food intolerance ↓ Diagnosis rests on linking specific foods to symptoms ↓ Take a food and symptom timing history
exam_trap: A, A commercial IgG food test - these are widely marketed and give official-looking results, but they are not recommended and do not diagnose intolerance.
takeaway: The key to assessing food intolerance is a careful history linking specific foods to the timing of symptoms.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis due to hepatitis C has routine bloods at his liver clinic review. His platelet count has fallen steadily over two years, while his haemoglobin and white cell count remain close to normal. On examination the spleen tip is palpable. He has no bleeding symptoms and takes no new medicines.

What is the most likely mechanism of his low platelet count?

options.A: Bone marrow infiltration by a malignancy

why_correct: Cirrhosis raises pressure in the portal venous system, causing congestive splenomegaly. The enlarged spleen sequesters platelets (hypersplenism), so a gradually falling platelet count with a palpable spleen in liver disease is most likely due to portal hypertension. Reduced hepatic thrombopoietin production can contribute. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Marrow infiltration would usually affect other cell lines and does not explain splenomegaly. B. Immune thrombocytopenia is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not cause splenomegaly. D. Folate deficiency would typically cause macrocytic anaemia too. E. DIC is an acute illness with bleeding and deranged clotting, not a slow decline in a well patient.
pearl: In chronic liver disease a falling platelet count is a useful marker of advanced fibrosis and portal hypertension.
thinking: Cirrhosis ↓ Slowly falling platelets with other counts preserved ↓ Palpable spleen ↓ Portal hypertension causes splenic congestion ↓ Hypersplenism sequesters platelets
exam_trap: B, Immune thrombocytopenia — isolated low platelets suggest ITP, but the cirrhosis and splenomegaly give a clear alternative explanation.
takeaway: Thrombocytopenia with splenomegaly in chronic liver disease usually reflects hypersplenism from portal hypertension.

stem:
A 61-year-old woman has a mildly raised ALT on two blood tests six months apart, found during a medication review. She feels well and drinks very little alcohol. She mentions that she needed a blood transfusion after a complicated delivery in the 1980s.

Which infection should be tested for?
why_correct: Hepatitis C is a blood-borne virus that becomes chronic in most people and can remain silent for decades while causing persistently raised transaminases. Current NHS advice is that anyone who had a blood transfusion in the UK before 1996 and has not been tested should be offered a hepatitis C test. Hepatitis C antibody testing with confirmatory RNA testing is appropriate, as curative antiviral treatment is available. Source: Hepatitis C (causes and treatment), NHS website, accessed October 2026.
why_wrong: A. Hepatitis A is spread faeco-orally and causes only acute infection. B. Hepatitis E is usually acute and self-limiting, becoming chronic mainly in immunosuppressed people. C. Epstein-Barr virus causes acute hepatitis with glandular fever, not years of silent enzyme rise. E. Cytomegalovirus does not cause chronic hepatitis in immunocompetent adults.
pearl: Hepatitis C is now treated with antiviral tablets taken for 8 to 12 weeks, which cure the infection in most people.
thinking: Persistently raised ALT in a well patient  ↓  Blood transfusion in the UK before 1996  ↓  Blood-borne virus that becomes chronic  ↓  Can be silent for decades  ↓  Test for hepatitis C
exam_trap: B, Hepatitis E — it can be transmitted by blood and can become chronic, but chronic infection is largely confined to immunosuppressed patients.
takeaway: Persistently raised liver enzymes in someone transfused in the UK before 1996 should prompt testing for hepatitis C.

stem:
A 69-year-old man who had a right hemicolectomy for caecal adenocarcinoma 18 months ago attends his surveillance appointment. He has lost weight and his liver blood tests have become deranged. CT shows several rounded lesions scattered through both lobes of the liver.

What is the most likely explanation?
why_correct: The liver is the commonest site of distant spread from colorectal cancer because venous blood from the bowel drains through the portal vein to the liver. Multiple lesions in both lobes, new deranged liver tests and weight loss in a man with previous bowel cancer make metastases most likely. He needs multidisciplinary review, as some colorectal liver metastases can be resected. Source: Colorectal cancer (NG151), NICE, 2020.
why_wrong: A. Hepatocellular carcinoma usually arises in a cirrhotic liver and is often a single dominant mass. C. Simple cysts are benign and do not cause weight loss or deranged liver tests. D. Liver abscesses usually present with fever and rigors. E. Haemangiomas are common benign incidental lesions and do not cause weight loss.
pearl: Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is used in colorectal cancer follow-up to monitor for recurrence, not for screening.
thinking: Previous colorectal cancer ↓ Weight loss and new deranged liver tests ↓ Multiple liver lesions in both lobes ↓ Portal venous drainage carries tumour to the liver ↓ Liver metastases
exam_trap: A, Hepatocellular carcinoma — a liver tumour is the obvious word, but multiple lesions in a non-cirrhotic liver after bowel cancer point to secondary, not primary, disease.
takeaway: New liver lesions after colorectal cancer are metastases until proven otherwise.

stem:
A hepatologist reviewing a man with long-standing cirrhosis wants a blood test that reflects how well the liver has been making proteins over the past few weeks, rather than over the past day or two.

Which test is most useful for this purpose?
why_correct: Albumin is made only by the liver and has a half-life of around three weeks, so a low level reflects reduced synthetic capacity over a longer period. This makes it useful for tracking chronic liver dysfunction, and it forms part of the Child-Pugh score. It can also be lowered by malnutrition, sepsis and protein loss, so it must be interpreted in context. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.
why_wrong: A. The prothrombin time reflects clotting factors with half-lives of hours, so it measures short-term synthetic function. B. ALT reflects hepatocyte injury, not synthetic function. D. Alkaline phosphatase indicates cholestasis or bone turnover. E. Creatine kinase is a marker of muscle injury.
pearl: Because clotting factor VII has a half-life of only a few hours, the INR is the best early marker of deteriorating synthetic function in acute liver failure.
thinking: Wants a measure of liver protein synthesis ↓ Over weeks rather than days ↓ Needs a long half-life liver-made protein ↓ INR is short-term ↓ Albumin
exam_trap: A, Prothrombin time — it is a true synthetic marker, but it reflects short-lived clotting factors and so changes over hours to days, not weeks.
takeaway: Albumin reflects longer-term hepatic synthetic function, whereas the INR reflects acute changes.

presentation: Prolonged prothrombin time in liver disease
stem:
A 52-year-old woman with decompensated alcohol-related cirrhosis is found on admission bloods to have a prolonged prothrombin time. She takes no anticoagulant, and the result does not improve after intravenous vitamin K.

Which process does this result most directly reflect?

options.A: Platelet sequestration within an enlarged spleen
options.C: Reduced hepatic production of clotting factors

correct_answer: C. Reduced hepatic production of clotting factors
why_correct: The liver synthesises most clotting factors, including factors II, VII, IX and X. When hepatocyte function fails, their production falls and the prothrombin time lengthens. Failure to correct with vitamin K shows the problem is synthetic failure rather than vitamin K deficiency, which is why the INR is a key prognostic marker in liver disease. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Splenic sequestration lowers the platelet count but does not affect the prothrombin time. B. Haemolysis does not prolong the prothrombin time. D. Marrow suppression lowers blood cell counts but does not alter clotting factor levels. E. Pancreatic enzymes have no role in clotting factor synthesis.
pearl: A prolonged prothrombin time that corrects with vitamin K suggests cholestasis or malnutrition rather than hepatocellular failure.
thinking: Prolonged prothrombin time in cirrhosis ↓ No anticoagulant ↓ No correction with vitamin K ↓ Not vitamin K deficiency ↓ Impaired hepatic clotting factor synthesis
exam_trap: A, Platelet sequestration — hypersplenism causes bleeding risk in cirrhosis, but platelets are not measured by the prothrombin time.
takeaway: A prolonged prothrombin time in liver disease that does not correct with vitamin K reflects failing clotting factor synthesis.

stem:
A 57-year-old man has type 2 diabetes, a greyish-bronze tan that he has all year round, and an enlarged liver. Genetic testing shows he is homozygous for the C282Y mutation in the HFE gene.

What process underlies his condition?

options.A: Excess iron absorption with tissue deposition
options.D: Autoimmune destruction of the small intrahepatic bile ducts

correct_answer: A. Excess iron absorption with tissue deposition
why_correct: Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder, most often due to homozygous C282Y HFE mutation, in which low hepcidin activity allows unregulated absorption of iron from the gut. The excess iron is deposited in the liver, pancreas, skin, heart, joints and pituitary, producing cirrhosis, diabetes and skin pigmentation. Source: Haemochromatosis, NICE Clinical Knowledge Summaries; BSG guidelines on HFE haemochromatosis, 2018.
why_wrong: B. Impaired biliary copper excretion is the mechanism of Wilson disease. C. Unconjugated bilirubin accumulation occurs in haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome. D. Autoimmune damage to small bile ducts describes primary biliary cholangitis. E. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes emphysema and liver disease without skin pigmentation or diabetes.
pearl: Venesection is the first-line treatment and, if started before cirrhosis develops, gives a normal life expectancy.
thinking: Diabetes, skin pigmentation and hepatomegaly ↓ Homozygous C282Y HFE mutation ↓ Hereditary haemochromatosis ↓ Unregulated gut iron absorption ↓ Iron deposition in organs
exam_trap: B, Defective biliary copper excretion — both are inherited metal storage disorders affecting the liver, but copper overload is Wilson disease, not haemochromatosis.
takeaway: Hereditary haemochromatosis is iron overload from excessive gut absorption, with deposition in liver, pancreas and skin.

stem:
A 16-year-old boy is brought to clinic by his parents because his school work has deteriorated, he has become irritable, and his handwriting has become shaky. Blood tests show raised transaminases and a low serum caeruloplasmin.

Build-up of which substance is responsible for his illness?
why_correct: Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of the ATP7B copper transporter, which impairs incorporation of copper into caeruloplasmin and its excretion into bile. Copper accumulates in the liver, then in the brain and cornea, causing hepatitis, psychiatric change and movement disorders in young people. Treatment is with a copper chelator such as penicillamine or trientine, or with zinc, which reduces copper absorption from the gut. Source: Wilson's disease, NHS website (nhs.uk), accessed October 2026.
why_wrong: B. Iron overload causes haemochromatosis, usually presenting in middle age with diabetes and pigmentation. C. Lead poisoning causes abdominal pain, anaemia and neuropathy but not low caeruloplasmin. D. Calcium accumulation is not the mechanism of this disease. E. Bilirubin may rise in liver disease but is not the underlying cause.
pearl: Wilson disease should be considered in anyone under about 40 with unexplained liver disease, or with liver disease plus neuropsychiatric symptoms.
thinking: Teenager with behavioural change and tremor ↓ Raised transaminases ↓ Low caeruloplasmin ↓ Wilson disease ↓ Copper accumulation
exam_trap: B, Iron — haemochromatosis is the more familiar metal storage liver disease, but it presents in middle age and does not lower caeruloplasmin.
takeaway: Wilson disease is copper accumulation from impaired biliary excretion, affecting liver, brain and cornea.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_correct: zinc reworded as reducing copper absorption, not listed as a chelator

stem:
A 49-year-old man who drinks heavily every day presents to the emergency department with two weeks of jaundice, a tender enlarged liver and a low-grade fever. Alcohol-related hepatitis is suspected.

Which liver blood test finding would most support this diagnosis?

options.A: ALT raised far more than AST
options.B: Raised unconjugated bilirubin with entirely normal enzymes
options.D: AST raised to a greater degree than ALT

correct_answer: D. AST raised to a greater degree than ALT
why_correct: Alcohol-related liver injury characteristically raises AST more than ALT, typically with a ratio of about two or more. Transaminases are usually only moderately raised, and GGT is typically high. Jaundice with tender hepatomegaly and fever in a heavy drinker, together with this pattern, supports alcohol-related hepatitis, whose severity is assessed with scores such as the Glasgow alcoholic hepatitis score. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.
why_wrong: A. ALT predominance is more typical of viral or drug-induced hepatitis. B. Isolated unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia suggests haemolysis or Gilbert syndrome. C. Transaminases in the thousands suggest ischaemic, viral or paracetamol injury rather than alcohol. E. GGT is typically raised with heavy alcohol use.
pearl: Alcohol depletes pyridoxal phosphate, which ALT depends on more than AST, partly explaining the AST-dominant pattern.
thinking: Heavy daily alcohol ↓ Jaundice, tender hepatomegaly and fever ↓ Suspected alcohol-related hepatitis ↓ Alcohol injury raises AST more than ALT ↓ AST greater than ALT
exam_trap: C, Transaminases in the thousands — severe illness suggests huge enzymes, but in alcohol-related hepatitis transaminases are only modestly raised.
takeaway: Alcohol-related hepatitis typically shows AST raised more than ALT with only modestly raised transaminases.

stem:
Pre-operative bloods for an elective hernia repair in a 60-year-old man come back with only one abnormality: a high alkaline phosphatase. Bilirubin and transaminases are within range and he feels well.

To decide whether liver or bone is the source, which blood test should be added?
why_correct: Alkaline phosphatase comes mainly from the liver and bone. GGT is produced by the hepatobiliary system but not by bone, so a raised GGT alongside ALP indicates a hepatobiliary source, whereas a normal GGT points towards bone. This guides whether to pursue liver imaging or bone causes such as Paget disease. Source: Guidelines on the management of abnormal liver blood tests, British Society of Gastroenterology, 2018.
why_wrong: A. Calcium may be abnormal in some bone diseases but does not establish the source of ALP. C. Creatine kinase reflects muscle damage. D. Amylase is used in pancreatic disease. E. Ferritin assesses iron stores and is an acute-phase reactant.
pearl: Alkaline phosphatase is physiologically raised in pregnancy (placental) and in growing adolescents (bone).
thinking: Isolated raised ALP ↓ Main sources are liver and bone ↓ GGT is hepatobiliary but not bony ↓ Raised GGT means liver source ↓ Check GGT
exam_trap: A, Serum calcium — it seems a natural bone test, but it is often normal in bone causes such as Paget disease and cannot localise the ALP.
takeaway: A raised GGT alongside a raised ALP indicates a hepatobiliary source rather than bone.

stem:
On a medical ward, a 70-year-old man with known cirrhosis has become disorientated and has a flapping tremor. His stool chart shows no bowel opening for four days since admission, and an infection screen is negative. The registrar asks the foundation doctor how the lack of bowel opening could explain his worsening mental state.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: A distended bowel compresses the portal vein and reduces liver blood flow
options.B: Faecal loading reduces carbohydrate absorption and causes hypoglycaemia
options.C: Straining at stool raises intracranial pressure
options.D: Slower transit lets colonic bacteria make and absorb more ammonia
options.E: Retained stool releases toxins that cause acute hepatocyte necrosis

correct_answer: D. Slower transit lets colonic bacteria make and absorb more ammonia
why_correct: Colonic bacteria break down protein and urea to produce ammonia and other nitrogenous compounds. When transit slows, more of these are generated and absorbed, and a cirrhotic liver with portosystemic shunting cannot clear them, so they reach the brain. This is why lactulose, which speeds transit and acidifies the colon to trap ammonia, is the first-line treatment. Source: Rifaximin for preventing episodes of overt hepatic encephalopathy (TA337), NICE, 2015.
why_wrong: A. Stool in the colon does not meaningfully compress the portal vein. B. Constipation does not reduce carbohydrate absorption enough to cause hypoglycaemia. C. Straining causes only brief pressure changes and does not explain encephalopathy. E. Constipation does not directly cause hepatocyte necrosis or acute liver failure.
pearl: Lactulose is converted by colonic bacteria to acids that lower colonic pH, converting ammonia to non-absorbable ammonium; rifaximin is added to prevent recurrence.
thinking: Cirrhosis with confusion and asterixis ↓ No bowel opening for several days ↓ Gut bacteria generate ammonia from nitrogenous material ↓ Slow transit increases production and absorption ↓ Failing liver and shunting let ammonia reach the brain
exam_trap: A, Compression of the portal vein — portal pressure is central to cirrhosis so a mechanical explanation sounds plausible, but the problem is increased ammonia load, not reduced liver blood flow.
takeaway: Constipation worsens hepatic encephalopathy by increasing gut ammonia production and absorption.

stem:
At his inflammatory bowel disease clinic, a 34-year-old man with ulcerative proctitis says that several times a day he feels he must rush to the toilet and strain, yet passes only a small amount of mucus and blood and is left feeling that his rectum is still not empty.

What is the term for this symptom?
why_correct: Tenesmus is a persistent or repeated urge to defecate with a feeling of incomplete evacuation, often with little or no stool passed. It reflects inflammation or a mass in the rectum, which is why it is typical of proctitis. His repeated straining with scanty output and a sense of a full rectum fits this exactly. Source: Ulcerative colitis (symptoms), NHS website (nhs.uk), accessed October 2026.
why_wrong: A. Steatorrhoea is pale, bulky, greasy stool from fat malabsorption. C. Haematochezia means passing fresh blood per rectum, which he has, but it does not describe the urge and sense of incomplete emptying. D. Odynophagia is pain on swallowing. E. Encopresis is repeated soiling by a child beyond toilet-training age, often from overflow around constipated stool.
pearl: New tenesmus in an older adult should prompt assessment for rectal cancer, as a rectal mass can produce the same sensation as inflammation.
thinking: Repeated urgent urge to open bowels ↓ Little passed despite straining ↓ Feeling the rectum is not empty ↓ Known rectal inflammation ↓ Symptom is tenesmus
exam_trap: C, Haematochezia — he does pass blood, so this is tempting, but the question asks for the name of the urge with incomplete evacuation, which is tenesmus.
takeaway: A frequent urge to defecate with a sense of incomplete emptying and little stool passed is tenesmus.

stem:
A 27-year-old man has had bloating and cramping lower abdominal pain on and off for a year. The pain eases after he opens his bowels, and he swings between constipation and loose motions. He asks his GP whether this could be something more serious.

Which additional feature in his history would most suggest inflammatory bowel disease rather than irritable bowel syndrome?

options.A: Pain that is relieved by defecation
options.C: Ongoing blood mixed with his stool
options.D: Bloating that worsens through the evening
options.E: Symptoms that flare at times of stress

correct_answer: C. Ongoing blood mixed with his stool
why_correct: Persistent rectal bleeding is not a feature of irritable bowel syndrome and suggests mucosal disease such as ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease. It should prompt blood tests, faecal calprotectin and referral rather than reassurance. The other features listed are all typical of irritable bowel syndrome. Source: Irritable bowel syndrome in adults (CG61), NICE, 2008, updated 2017; Faecal calprotectin diagnostic tests (DG11), NICE, 2013.
why_wrong: A. Pain relieved by opening the bowels is one of the core features supporting irritable bowel syndrome. B. Passage of mucus is recognised in irritable bowel syndrome and is listed by NICE as a supportive feature. D. Bloating that worsens through the day is typical of irritable bowel syndrome. E. Stress commonly aggravates irritable bowel syndrome.
pearl: Faecal calprotectin helps separate inflammatory bowel disease from irritable bowel syndrome in adults with lower GI symptoms when cancer is not suspected.
thinking: Pain eased by defecation with altered habit ↓ Pattern fits irritable bowel syndrome ↓ Look for features that IBS does not explain ↓ Ongoing rectal bleeding implies mucosal disease ↓ Raise concern for inflammatory bowel disease
exam_trap: B, Passing mucus — mucus sounds like a sign of inflammation, but it is common in irritable bowel syndrome and does not by itself point to inflammatory bowel disease.
takeaway: Persistent rectal bleeding is a red flag that is not explained by irritable bowel syndrome.

stem:
A 29-year-old teacher was recently diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome after normal blood tests, coeliac serology and faecal calprotectin. At a follow-up appointment with her GP she asks whether the condition is damaging her bowel or could turn into cancer.

Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: It causes patchy inflammation through the full thickness of the bowel wall
options.B: It causes mucosal changes that increase the risk of bowel cancer
options.C: It alters gut function and sensitivity without damaging the bowel
options.D: It gradually scars and narrows the colon over time
options.E: It produces shallow ulcers that bleed from time to time

correct_answer: C. It alters gut function and sensitivity without damaging the bowel
why_correct: Irritable bowel syndrome is a disorder of gut-brain interaction, involving altered motility and heightened visceral sensitivity without inflammation, ulceration or structural damage. Once the diagnosis is secure, it is not associated with a long-term increase in the risk of colorectal cancer or inflammatory bowel disease. Explaining this clearly is an important part of management and helps reduce anxiety. Source: British Society of Gastroenterology guidelines on the management of irritable bowel syndrome, BSG, 2021; Irritable bowel syndrome in adults (CG61), NICE, 2008, updated 2017.
why_wrong: A. Patchy transmural inflammation describes Crohn's disease. B. Irritable bowel syndrome does not raise colorectal cancer risk. D. Fibrotic strictures occur with Crohn's disease or ischaemia, not irritable bowel syndrome. E. Mucosal ulceration and bleeding suggest inflammatory bowel disease.
pearl: First-line management of irritable bowel syndrome is lifestyle and dietary advice, with antispasmodics, laxatives or loperamide for predominant symptoms and low-dose tricyclics if these fail.
thinking: Diagnosis of irritable bowel syndrome after normal tests ↓ Patient worried about bowel damage and cancer ↓ IBS is a functional disorder ↓ No inflammation, ulceration or stricturing ↓ No increased cancer risk
exam_trap: B, Mucosal changes raising cancer risk — long-term bowel conditions such as colitis do raise cancer risk, so this seems plausible, but irritable bowel syndrome causes no mucosal damage.
takeaway: Irritable bowel syndrome is a functional disorder that does not damage the bowel or increase cancer risk.
